title: Common Behavioural Problems in Children and Growth Monitoring
introduction: Behaviour is a primary channel through which children communicate emotions, stress, and developmental challenges, while routine growth monitoring provides an objective early-warning system for nutritional, systemic, and endocrine disorders. Mastering non-stigmatizing behavioural assessment alongside accurate anthropometric plotting equips nurses to protect both child mental health and physical survival.
learningOutcomes: 3.1 Distinguish developmentally expected childhood behaviours from clinically significant psychosocial, habit, anxiety, disruptive/ADHD, and sleep disorders.
3.2 Outline assessment strategies, therapeutic communication, family interventions, and red flags requiring urgent referral in childhood behavioural care.

3.3 Define growth monitoring and growth assessment, explain their primary and secondary aims, and describe the core anthropometric parameters (weight, length/height, head circumference, MUAC, BMI-for-age).
3.4 Demonstrate accurate measurement procedures, WHO Z-score growth chart plotting and interpretation, and recommended monitoring intervals from birth to 18 years.
3.5 Identify growth faltering, undernutrition classifications (underweight, stunting, wasting), age-specific referral criteria, and practical solutions to growth monitoring challenges.

content.heading: Psychosocial Disorders and Habit Disorders in Children
content.body: A psychosocial disorder is a mental health condition influenced by life experiences and maladjusted cognitive/behavioural processes, shaped by child temperament, family stability, school/peers, and community conditions. Rather than labelling isolated behaviours quickly, clinicians evaluate persistence, severity, developmental appropriateness, cross-setting occurrence, and functional impairment. Psychological disorders manifest across four domains: emotions (sadness, anxiety, depression), behaviour (aggression, defiance, regression), physical function (psychogenic headaches/abdominal pain, feeding/sleep impairment in younger children), and mental performance (poor school performance/concentration). Causes include inconsistent parenting, marital conflict, abuse/neglect, overindulgence, chronic illness, and separation/bereavement; anticipatory guidance helps prepare children for stressful events like elective surgery. Habit disorders are repetitive, often tension-reducing or self-soothing behaviours—including thumb-sucking (normal in early infancy; persistent sucking may misalign teeth; manage by ignoring and reassuring), nail-biting, hair-pulling, skin-picking, body-rocking, head-banging, air-swallowing, breath-holding, and tics (sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic motor/vocal movements of head, neck, or hands that disappear during sleep, distinguishing them from dystonias/dyskinesias; parental pressure worsens tics). Stuttering is not tension-reducing; it occurs in 5% of children learning to speak (more common in boys; ~20% persist into adulthood), usually resolves if initially ignored, and warrants speech-therapy referral if persistent. Elimination concerns include enuresis (repeated involuntary urination—primary vs. secondary after a dry period) and encopresis (repeated inappropriate stool passage, often linked to chronic constipation/overflow soiling); nurses screen for UTI, constipation, or diabetes, protect dignity without shaming, and use supportive routines and positive reinforcement.

content.heading: Anxiety Disorders, Disruptive Behaviour, ADHD, Sleep Problems, and Nursing Care
content.body: While transient fears are normal, ~6–7% of children develop clinically impairing anxiety disorders—including separation anxiety, specific phobia, social anxiety, generalized anxiety disorder, panic symptoms, OCD, selective mutism, and school phobia (1–2% of children, ~75% with co-occurring depression/anxiety). Anxiety presents across thoughts ('what-if' worries), feelings (dread, irritability), body (stomach-ache, palpitations, tremor), and behaviour (avoidance, clinginess, school refusal). First-line management combines psychoeducation, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) with gradual exposure, calm caregiver validation without reinforcing avoidance, and school liaison. Disruptive behaviours like toddler temper tantrums or breath-holding stem from frustration (avoid punitive reactions; ensure safety and later comfort), whereas persistent truancy, arson, and severe aggression are abnormal. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)—diagnosed in 3–7% of school-age children—features inattention, motor overactivity, and impulsiveness evident before age 7, lasting >6 months across home and school, and impairing function; management includes specialist-initiated methylphenidate, family behavioural therapy, and possibly essential fatty acids. Sleep problems (too little, too much, poor quality, insomnia, nightmares with recall, sleep terrors without recall, sleepwalking, sleep-disordered breathing/snoring with apnoea, or adolescent circadian delay) impair cognition, behaviour, and weight. AASM recommended sleep durations: 1–2 yrs (11–14 hrs), 3–5 yrs (10–13 hrs), 6–12 yrs (9–12 hrs), and 13–18 yrs (8–10 hrs); by 1–3 months longest sleep shifts to night, though 30% still wake at night at 1 year. Interventions prioritize consistent wind-down routines, screen removal, 1–2 week sleep diaries, and behavioural methods (unmodified/modified extinction, positive routines); hypnotics are avoided (except brief use in night terrors/sleepwalking), while specialist-supervised melatonin may help in autism, ADHD, cerebral palsy, or visual impairment. Urgent red flags requiring immediate action include suicidal/self-harm thoughts, suspected abuse/neglect, severe agitation/psychosis, seizure-like events, snoring with apnoea/cyanosis, and new bedwetting with polyuria/polydipsia.

content.heading: Growth Monitoring: Meaning, Aims, Anthropometric Parameters, and Measurement Techniques
content.body: Growth monitoring is the routine, periodic measurement, plotting, and interpretation of a child's physical size over time to detect growth deviations, undernutrition (especially severe protein-energy malnutrition), overnutrition, and chronic systemic or endocrine disease before the child looks visibly ill. Its primary aim is early detection of abnormal growth; secondary aims include counselling caregivers on feeding, hygiene, and immunization, allaying parental anxiety, and sensitizing clinicians to use growth charts. Five key anthropometric parameters are assessed: (1) Weight (kg, read to nearest 0.1 kg on a zeroed scale with shoes/heavy clothing removed)—most sensitive indicator of recent/acute health; doubles by ~5 months and triples by 1 year; (2) Length/Height (cm)—reflects long-term nutrition; children <2 years are measured lying flat on a length board (two assistants), while children ≥2 years stand barefoot against a stadiometer with heels, buttocks, shoulders, and head touching (~50 cm at birth, ~75 cm at 1 year; falling below 90% of median indicates stunting); (3) Head Circumference (cm, largest of 3 readings above eyebrows and occiput, ~35 cm at birth to ~46 cm at 1 year)—tracks brain growth in the first 2–3 years, with normal arm-to-head circumference ratio ~0.33; (4) Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC, 6–59 months, midpoint of relaxed left upper arm)—remains fairly stable from ages 1–5 (median 16.5 cm; early malnutrition warning 12.5–13.5 cm; IMNCI colour tape: <11.5 cm red = severe malnutrition, 11.5 to <12.5 cm yellow = moderate, ≥12.5 cm green = normal); and (5) Weight-for-Height / BMI-for-Age—assesses body proportion and wasting/overweight without requiring exact age for weight-for-height.

content.heading: WHO Growth Charts, Z-Scores, Monitoring Intervals, and Interpreting Curves
content.body: WHO Child Growth Standards provide sex-specific charts (weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-length/height, BMI-for-age, head circumference-for-age) displaying Z-score (standard deviation) lines: +3, +2, +1, 0 (median), -1, -2, and -3 SD (on classic WHO cards, the upper curve marks the 50th percentile for boys and the lower marks the 3rd percentile for girls). Indicators classify status: low Weight-for-Age (<-2 SD) = Underweight; low Length/Height-for-Age (<-2 SD) = Stunting (chronic undernutrition); low Weight-for-Length/Height (<-2 SD; <-3 SD severe) = Wasting (acute weight loss); high BMI-for-Age (>+2 SD) = Overweight/Obesity. Proper chart usage includes recording identity and accurate DOB on visit 1, explaining and keeping the chart with parents in a plastic sleeve, measuring parents' heights to project target height at 18 years (with 3rd–97th centile bands), marking points strictly as dots (not circles), and joining consecutive dots to inspect trajectory direction—not merely one isolated dot. A rising curve parallel to reference lines shows healthy growth, whereas a flat, falling, or downward-crossing curve signals growth faltering (caused by poor feeding, recurrent infections like diarrhoea/malaria/pneumonia, low birth weight, poverty, poor hygiene, or chronic HIV/TB). Recommended monitoring intervals: manual guidelines specify once fortnightly (<6 months), monthly (6–18 months), every 6 months (>18 months), and yearly from age 6–18 years (with BMI, penile length, and sexual maturity rating [SMR] assessed yearly from 6 years; lecture summary also highlights monthly for 0–12 mos, every 3 mos for 1–2 yrs, every 6 mos for 2–5 yrs, and more often when sick/faltering).

content.heading: Criteria for Referral, Assess-Analyse-Act, and Overcoming Challenges
content.body: Clinical referral criteria are age-stratified: (1) First 3 years—length/height, weight, or head circumference <3rd or >97th percentile; crossing two major percentile lines upward or downward; height outside mid-parental range; weight loss/no gain for 1 month (<6 mos) or 2–3 months (6–12 mos); micropenis, undescended testes, or ambiguous genitalia; (2) Ages 3–9 years—height outside mid-parental range, BMI >85th percentile, growth rate <5 cm/year, precocious puberty (girls with breast budding/pubic/axillary hair <8 yrs; boys with pubic/axillary hair or genital/testicular enlargement <9 yrs), craniospinal irradiation/brain tumour surgery, or micropenis; (3) Ages 9–18 years—height <3rd or >97th percentile, crossing two major percentile lines, BMI >85th percentile, pubertal arrest >2 years, gynecomastia in boys, hirsutism/menstrual irregularities in girls, or delayed puberty (girls: no breast budding by 14 yrs or no menarche by 15 yrs; boys: no puberty signs by 16 yrs). Whenever abnormal growth appears, nurses apply the Assess–Analyse–Act cycle: verify/repeat measurements, review prior charts, evaluate breastfeeding/complementary diet, screen for illness and bilateral pitting oedema, counsel caregivers (exclusive breastfeeding 0–6 mos, nutritious complementary food ≥6 mos, extra feeding during illness, immunization, vitamin A, deworming, safe water/handwashing), treat/refer per protocol, and schedule close follow-up. Overcoming growth monitoring barriers (uncalibrated/missing equipment, inaccurate age determination, poor staff training, incomplete documentation, low caregiver attendance, food insecurity) demands regular training/supervision, functional calibrated equipment, community mobilization, effective counselling, and strong referral follow-up.

inTextQuestions.question: How can childhood tics be clinically differentiated from dystonias and dyskinetic movements?
inTextQuestions.answer: Tics are absent during sleep, whereas dystonias and dyskinetic movements are not characterized by complete absence in sleep; additionally, tics are sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic, and worsen under parental pressure.

inTextQuestions.question: What are the diagnostic criteria for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) regarding age of onset, duration, and settings?
inTextQuestions.answer: Symptoms (inattention, motor overactivity, impulsiveness) must be evident before age 7 years, persist for more than 6 months, occur in both home and school settings, and impede the child's functioning.

inTextQuestions.question: How is a child under 2 years old measured for linear growth compared to a child aged 2 years and older?
inTextQuestions.answer: Children under 2 years are measured lying flat (recumbent length) on a length board with two people assisting, whereas children 2 years and older are measured standing barefoot (height) against a vertical stadiometer.

inTextQuestions.question: What nutritional condition is indicated by a Weight-for-Length/Height Z-score below -2 SD versus a Length/Height-for-Age Z-score below -2 SD?
inTextQuestions.answer: Weight-for-Length/Height below -2 SD indicates Wasting (acute/recent weight loss; below -3 SD is severe), whereas Length/Height-for-Age below -2 SD indicates Stunting (chronic/long-term undernutrition).

saqs.question: List the four areas in which psychological disorders manifest in children and state five examples of tension-reducing habit disorders.
saqs.answer: Psychological disorders manifest in emotions (anxiety, depression), behaviour (aggression), physical function (psychogenic complaints), and mental performance (school difficulties). Five tension-reducing habit disorders are thumb-sucking, nail-biting, hair-pulling, head-banging, and tics (also body-rocking, air-swallowing, breath-holding, repetitive vocalizations).

saqs.question: Outline three behavioural approaches to managing pediatric sleep problems and state the AASM recommended sleep durations for ages 1–2 years, 3–5 years, 6–12 years, and 13–18 years.
saqs.answer: Behavioural strategies include unmodified extinction (ignoring cries while monitoring safety), modified extinction (ignoring for specified intervals), and positive routines (quiet pre-sleep wind-down with positive parent-child interaction), alongside consistent bedtimes and removing bedroom screens. Recommended durations: 1–2 yrs (11–14 hrs), 3–5 yrs (10–13 hrs), 6–12 yrs (9–12 hrs), and 13–18 yrs (8–10 hrs).

saqs.question: Explain the primary and secondary aims of growth monitoring and describe the clinical significance of weight, height, head circumference, and MUAC.
saqs.answer: Primary aim: identify growth deviations (undernutrition, overnutrition, or disease). Secondary aims: counsel parents on feeding/hygiene/immunization to allay anxiety and encourage clinicians to use growth charts. Weight reflects recent/acute health; height-for-age reflects long-term nutrition (stunting); head circumference tracks brain growth in the first 2–3 years; MUAC (6–59 mos) rapidly screens acute malnutrition (<11.5 cm severe, 11.5–<12.5 cm moderate).

saqs.question: State the recommended intervals for growth monitoring from birth to 18 years and describe the key steps in plotting a child's weight on a WHO growth chart.
saqs.answer: Recommended intervals: under 6 months (once fortnightly), 6–18 months (monthly), after 18 months (every 6 months), and from 6–18 years (yearly, including BMI and SMR). Plotting steps: select the sex-specific chart, confirm completed age in months and date, weigh accurately, locate age on horizontal axis and weight on vertical axis, mark a dot (not a circle) at their intersection, join to the previous dot, and interpret the trajectory direction.

saqs.question: Identify four growth-chart referral criteria for children in the first 3 years of life and four criteria for adolescents aged 9–18 years.
saqs.answer: First 3 years: measurements <3rd or >97th percentile, crossing two major percentile lines, weight loss/no gain for 1 month (<6 mos) or 2–3 months (6–12 mos), and micropenis/undescended testes/ambiguous genitalia. Ages 9–18 years: height <3rd or >97th percentile or crossing two major lines, BMI >85th percentile, pubertal arrest >2 years, and delayed puberty (girls: no breast budding by 14 yrs or no menarche by 15 yrs; boys: no puberty signs by 16 yrs).
